area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a steep bank changes lift, load factor and control forces, teach the entry, roll-out and recovery of a steep turn on round dials, on glass and on partial panel, coach the cross-check, coordination and trim it needs, fly it from the right seat while explaining it, and analyze and correct the pitch, bank, power, precession, coordination and trim errors an examiner simulates.
why: Steep turns by instruments build cross-check, interpretation and control, and they prepare a pilot to react smoothly, quickly and confidently to an unexpected abnormal attitude in cloud [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. At about 45° of bank or more the airplane keeps rolling on its own [[24:73|AFH 3-12]], and past 45° extra back pressure tightens the turn instead of raising the nose [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]: that is how a sloppy steep turn becomes a diving spiral [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. The CFII PTS asks you to teach it full panel and partial panel, fly it while explaining it, and fix the errors an examiner flies on purpose (CFII PTS, Area VI, Task G).

warmup: Think first: your instrument student flies tidy standard-rate turns. In her first 45° steep turn under the hood the altimeter unwinds 150 feet, she pulls harder, the bank creeps to 55° and the airspeed climbs. You take control and roll out, and the attitude indicator shows wings level while the heading keeps creeping. Which three things went wrong, and which would you fix first?

key_terms.def: Any turn greater than standard rate; the exact bank where a turn becomes steep is unimportant [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. The IFH glass example uses 45° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].
The part of total lift that opposes weight in a bank. To hold altitude the pilot raises the angle of attack with back pressure so it still balances weight [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
The ratio of lift to weight [[23:89|IFH 4-12]], expressed in Gs [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]. In a level turn it depends only on bank: 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

At about 45° or more the airplane keeps rolling into the turn with neutral controls, because the outer wing flies faster and makes more lift; hold opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
In the IFH steep turn, a bank past 50°. Pilots tend to do it in early steep turn training [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].
Altimeter and VSI moving rapidly down with the airspeed rising despite back pressure, after overbanking without enough pitch [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].
Steep turns are flown at or below it because of the higher load factors [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. VA is lower when the airplane is light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: a 50-knot stall becomes 60 knots in a level 45° turn and 70 knots at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

The tilting or turning of a gyro in response to a deflective force [[1:217|PHAK 8-15]]. Bearing friction makes the attitude gyro precess, and an erection mechanism pushes it back upright [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
A small bank and pitch error after a 180° turn that corrects itself within a minute or so after returning to straight-and-level flight [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
Starting the roll-out before the heading: about 20° early in the IFH 45° steep turn [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], or half the bank by the AFH rule [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
Ball toward the inside of the turn: slipping. Ball toward the outside: skidding [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

chunks.title: What Task G asks, and how it is tested

body.p: **Teaching steep turns** is Task G of Area VI. You describe the full panel and partial panel entry and recovery, the need for a proper instrument cross-check, the roll-in and roll-out, and coordination of control and trim; then four common errors; then you demonstrate while explaining, and analyze and correct errors the evaluator simulates (CFII PTS, Area VI, Task G). The Area NOTE makes Task H mandatory plus at least one other Task, so Task G may or may not be picked (CFII PTS, Area VI NOTE).

What the IFH means by steep: for instrument training in conventional airplanes, any turn greater than standard rate is steep, and the exact bank where a turn becomes steep is unimportant. What matters is learning to control the airplane at banks beyond those normally used on instruments [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Normal standard-rate banks run 10° to 20° [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]; the IFH glass example rolls into 45° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

Why you teach it: steep turns sharpen cross-check, interpretation and control, and they prepare the pilot for smooth, quick and confident reactions to unexpected abnormal attitudes in instrument conditions [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The IFH notes that the instrument practical test standards do not call for steep turns on the checkride, but that does not remove the need for the student to show proficiency to an instructor [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

callout.text: Application: the IFH says steep turns are entered, held and recovered the same way as shallower turns [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Brief it that way: "Same turn, more bank, more back pressure, more power, and a faster scan."

check.q: Your student read in the IFH that steep turns are not on the instrument checkride and asks why she must practice them. What do you answer?
check.a: The IFH says that does not remove the need to show proficiency to an instructor [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], and steep turn practice prepares her to react smoothly and confidently to an unexpected abnormal attitude in cloud [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

chunks.title: Lift, load factor and stall speed in a steep bank

body.p: **Start with the physics.** In a level turn total lift splits into a vertical part and a horizontal part. To hold altitude the pilot raises the angle of attack with back pressure so the vertical part still balances weight, and adds power for the extra drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The steeper the bank, the more lift goes sideways; once the bank passes 45° the horizontal component is the greater force [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

bullets: Load factor is the same for a given bank in any level turn, whatever the airplane or airspeed: 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60°. At 2.0 the airplane and everyone in it effectively weigh twice as much [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
It rises at a terrific rate after 45° or 50° of bank [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. A level turn at 75° exceeds the 3.8 load factor a standard category GA airplane is designed for [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. An airplane that stalls at 50 knots in level flight stalls at 60 knots in a level 45° turn and at 70 knots at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

So steep turns are flown at or below VA or VO; at or below that speed the airplane stalls before it exceeds the design load limit [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. VA is lower at light weight, for example 90 knots instead of 100 [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Once the bank is set, considerable elevator force is needed to hold level flight [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: On the panel this shows up as pitch trouble. Because the vertical lift component is greatly reduced, pitch control is usually the hardest part of the maneuver [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The pitch increase needed is usually no more than 3° to 5°, depending on the airplane [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

callout.text: 45°: 1.41 G, a 50-knot stall becomes 60. 60°: 2 G, it becomes 70 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Pitch up 3° to 5° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

check.q: Your student says a 45° steep turn must pull more G in the club's fast airplane than in the trainer. What do you tell her?
check.a: In a level turn the load factor depends on bank alone: 1.41 at 45° in any airplane at any airspeed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Airspeed changes the rate and radius of the turn, not the load factor [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

body.p: **Why the bank keeps growing.** The AFH sorts turns by stability. Below about 20° the airplane slowly levels its own wings. Between about 20° and 45° it holds the bank with neutral aileron. At about 45° or more it keeps rolling into the turn unless the pilot holds opposite aileron, and how much depends on bank and airspeed [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

The cause is the turn radius. The outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it flies faster and makes more lift, which rolls the airplane further into the turn. Hold opposite aileron once the bank you want is reached. The faster outer wing also makes more drag, which causes a slight slip in steep turns; correct it with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. The IFH adds that as the outboard wing travels faster it makes a greater and greater lift differential compared to the inboard wing [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

Airplanes differ. Some are very stable in turns and need only slight trim; others need a constant, rapid cross-check and control to stop overbanking [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Pilots in early steep turn training tend to overbank, and the IFH calls a bank past 50° overbanking [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. On round dials the student sees the bank pointer creep past the 45° mark; at the same airspeed, more bank also means a faster rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so the heading indicator speeds up too.

callout.text: Application: show the tendency once in VMC before the hood goes on. Establish 45°, relax the aileron pressure for a moment so the student can watch the bank pointer move past 45°, then stop it with opposite aileron. Agree on a bank limit in the briefing, well short of 60°.

check.q: Your student holds 45° by keeping a little aileron into the turn, as she does at 20°. What happens, and what do you teach?
check.a: At about 45° or more the airplane keeps rolling with neutral controls, so aileron into the turn steepens it further. Once the bank is set she must hold opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

chunks.title: Full panel on round dials: entry and the established turn

body.p: **Procedure using full panel for entry** on analog instruments: enter as for a shallower turn, but prepare to cross-check rapidly as the turn steepens [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

bullets: Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder. Pilots commonly roll in much too fast; early on, base the roll rate on how fast the student can cross-check and interpret [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
Set the bank on the attitude indicator. The IFH example dial has bank lines at 10°, 20°, 30°, 45° and 60° [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]; some dials are graduated only every 30° [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

As the bank comes in, the loss of vertical lift moves the altimeter, VSI and airspeed needles quickly unless pitch comes up at once, and the faster the roll, the more sudden the change. A cross-check fast enough to see the need lets smooth, steady back pressure hold altitude [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].
Power: the power for a constant airspeed increases as bank and drag increase. With practice the power for each bank is learned, so it needs little attention [[23:184|IFH 7-23]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].
Established: attend to the most important tasks first and keep the pitch attitude relatively constant, which frees time to cross-check and interpret [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

body.p: Read Figure 7-36 with the student: a steep left bank on the attitude indicator, the turn coordinator's miniature airplane past the standard-rate mark with the ball centered, and the altimeter and VSI steady. The turn coordinator shows only rate and direction of turn, not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], so in a steep turn it confirms direction, rate and coordination, and the bank comes from the attitude indicator.

Which instrument is primary? The IFH labels no primary instruments for the steep turn. It does say the attitude indicator is primary when flying a specific bank or pitch angle [[23:199|IFH 7-38]], that the altimeter is normally primary for pitch in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]], and that at a constant airspeed in a turn the airspeed indicator is primary for power [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Application: in primary-and-supporting words, teach attitude indicator for bank, altimeter for pitch and airspeed for power once the turn is established.

callout.text: If pitch control is consistently late on entries, roll out to straight-and-level at once and analyze. Practice shallower turns first, then increase the bank as a quicker and more accurate cross-check and control develop [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

check.q: In a 45° left turn your student calls the turn coordinator her primary bank instrument, as in a standard-rate turn. What do you tell her?
check.a: The turn coordinator shows only rate and direction, not bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], and it is already past the standard-rate mark. For a specific bank angle the IFH makes the attitude indicator primary [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

chunks.title: Full panel on glass: the IFH 45° steep turn, step by step

body.p: The IFH glass section gives the clearest procedure. A PFD has a 45° index on the roll scale, so the pilot can roll precisely to 45° instead of estimating it [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

head: IFH step
What to teach with it
rows: 1. Perform clearing turns [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Under the hood the lookout is yours. Failure to clear before and while maneuvering is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (CFII PTS, Unsatisfactory Performance)
2. Roll left into a 45° bank and immediately raise the pitch about 3° to 5° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Vertical lift starts to drop as soon as the bank increases; left alone, the altimeter, VSI tape and altitude trend show a pronounced loss and the airspeed rises [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
3. As the bank rolls past 30°, add power to hold the entry airspeed [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
The higher angle of attack adds drag [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
4. Trim off the aft control wheel forces [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Once trimmed the turn is virtually hands-off, which leaves more time to cross-check [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
5. Start the roll-out about 20° before the desired heading [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Same roll rate as the roll-in, so the lead stays predictable [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
6. Forward pressure to the level cruise pitch attitude [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
The vertical lift component increases during the roll-out; not lowering the pitch gives a consistent altitude gain [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
7. Reduce power to the entry setting [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Back pressure released and power reduced, in proportion to the changing aerodynamic forces [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]
8. Retrim as soon as practical, or roll into a right steep turn and continue from step 3 [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
The reversal shows whether pitch, power and trim come out and go back in on time
9. Establish cruise and complete the checklist items [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]
Back to the straight-and-level scan

body.p: Altitude corrections: the IFH calls it imperative to change the bank by ±5° to vary the vertical lift, not just adjust back pressure, and to do both at once. All the trend indicators, the VSI, altimeter and airspeed belong in the scan [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

Glass also flags an overbank. On the IFH example PFD, past 60° of bank the roll index extends to show the shortest way back to wings level, and at 65° the display declutters until the bank is back under 60° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With a working AHRS there is no precession error [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

callout.text: Application: the 45° index makes bank easy, so glass students tend to nail the bank and then watch the altitude drift. Put pitch in every callout: "Forty-five, nose up, power."

check.q: On a PFD your student is 80 feet low in a 45° left turn and keeps pulling harder. What does the IFH want her to do?
check.a: Shallow the bank about 5° and adjust the back pressure at the same time, to increase the vertical component of lift [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. Past 45°, pulling alone mostly tightens the turn [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

body.p: **Roll-in/roll-out procedure.** Use coordinated aileron and rudder, at a roll rate the student's cross-check can keep up with; maneuvering faster than that only creates the need for corrections [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. In a steep turn this matters more, because the faster the bank changes, the more suddenly the lift changes [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

bullets: Roll-in: pitch up as the bank comes in, about 3° to 5°, and power as the bank passes 30° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The AFH has back pressure and power coming in generally before 30° of bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Lead: the IFH glass procedure starts the roll-out about 20° before the heading [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The AFH rule is half the bank: a right turn at 60° that began on 270° rolls out starting at 240° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. The IFH turn rule is also half the bank, adjusted once the student's own roll-out technique is known [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

Roll-out: elevator and power are coordinated with the bank in proportion to the changing forces: back pressure released and power reduced [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Vary the aft force with the power to arrive back at the entry altitude, heading and airspeed [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].
Same rate both ways: matching roll-in and roll-out rates makes the lead predictable [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Trim: if it was used, take out the trim and the power as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; retrim as soon as practical [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

body.p: Errors are more exaggerated, harder to correct and harder to analyze unless the rates of entry and recovery match the student's skill in cross-check, interpretation and control [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. That sentence is your lesson plan: slow roll rates first, faster ones as the scan keeps up.

callout.text: Roll in: bank, nose up, power past 30°, trim. Roll out about 20° early: bank off, nose down, power back, trim [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

check.q: After every roll-out your student ends up 100 feet high. What is the cause, and what do you teach?
check.a: Failure to lower the pitch as the vertical lift returns during the roll-out [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Back pressure must be released and power reduced in step with the bank [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

chunks.title: Partial panel: round dials and glass standby instruments

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel.** Every basic maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown with the attitude and heading indicators covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and on glass with the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. The PTS wants both because instrument-rated pilots have died maneuvering in cloud with failed gyros or a lost display (CFII PTS, Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills).

Round dials, gyros covered
Glass, AHRS failed (IFH example)

Turn coordinator: roll rate while rolling, then rate of turn; no bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]] and no pitch [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]
Standby attitude indicator, which can tumble at high bank angles or extreme pitch [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
Pitch
Altimeter: the needle's speed shows the size of the error; VSI trend; airspeed [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]

Altitude and VSI tapes still work with only the AHRS failed [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]; standby altimeter and airspeed indicator if the air data computer fails too [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]; no abrupt yoke movements [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]
Coordination

Heading
Clock, then the compass once level [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Magnetic compass; timed turns are simpler than compass turns [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]

body.p: What a partial panel steep turn is: any turn greater than standard rate counts as steep for instrument training [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], so on round dials it means holding the turn coordinator's miniature airplane past the standard-rate mark. At a given airspeed more bank gives a faster rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so that deflection stands in for the bank. No source gives the turn coordinator picture for a particular bank angle.

Pitch is harder without the attitude indicator. The rate of the altimeter needle tells how big the pitch error is [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. With limited instruments only small, precise inputs work; rapid ones set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot and fix her on the altimeter [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

callout.text: Application: keep partial panel steep turns modest, only somewhat past standard rate, and on glass stay inside the standby attitude indicator's limits in the AFM supplement. The turn coordinator cannot show bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], and the analog standby gyro can tumble at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Recovering from a spiral on partial panel is taught in FII.VI.H.

check.q: Gyros covered, your student holds the turn coordinator well past the standard-rate mark, and the altimeter starts down slowly. How should she judge the correction?
check.a: By the needle's rate: slow movement means a small pitch error and a small correction [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Small, precise inputs only, because rapid ones cause oscillation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

chunks.title: The need for a proper instrument cross-check

body.p: **The need for a proper instrument cross-check.** Aerodynamic forces change sharply at steeper banks, and skill in cross-check, interpretation and control is needed in proportion [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Steep turns teach the pilot to recognize and adapt to rapidly changing forces that demand a faster cross-check of all flight instruments [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

bullets: Build the scan first. A comprehensive scan should exist before steep turn training starts, and all the trend indicators, the VSI, altimeter and airspeed are essential [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].
Speed it up on entry. Cross-check rapidly as the turn steepens [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; catch the need for pitch at once and smooth, steady back pressure holds the altitude [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].
Spread it out when established. Keep the pitch relatively constant and do the most important tasks first, which leaves time to cross-check and interpret [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

Do not drop instruments at the roll-out. A pilot who levels from a 180° steep turn on the attitude indicator alone, without checking the heading indicator, misses the small precession error [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
The key: a thorough understanding of the aerodynamics plus a quick and reliable cross-check [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

body.p: How to teach it: have the student say the scan aloud. When she thinks aloud you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Start with shallower turns, learn the attitude changes and control responses, then increase the bank as the cross-check gets quicker and more accurate [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

callout.text: Application: a scan call for the established turn: "Bank forty-five, altimeter, VSI, airspeed, ball." Repeat it until the eyes move without the words.

check.q: Why does the IFH want a comprehensive scan in place before steep turn training begins?
check.a: The forces change faster in a steep turn and demand a faster cross-check of all the instruments [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], and the trend indicators, VSI, altimeter and airspeed are all essential to fly it by instruments alone [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

body.p: **Coordination of control and trim.** Three things push the ball off center in a steep turn:

bullets: Adverse yaw on entry and roll-out: aileron deflection adds drag on the rising wing and yaws the nose away from the turn; rudder applied with the aileron counters it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
The faster outer wing's extra drag, which causes a slight slip in steep turns; correct it with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Left-turning tendencies such as P-factor, which need effective rudder and aileron coordination [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: Reading the ball: toward the inside of the turn is a slip, toward the outside a skid [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. A slipping airplane is banked too much for its rate of turn: add rudder on the side of the ball or reduce the bank. A skid means too much rate for the bank: relax rudder toward the turn or increase the bank [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. Check the ball throughout the turn, especially if pressures are held instead of trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Trim: the IFH says to use trim so control forces are not held for any length of time; once trimmed, the turn is virtually hands-off, which leaves more time for the cross-check. With time and practice an instructor can demonstrate steep turns with and without trim [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The AFH notes that the certification standards do not specify trim for steep turns: it depends on the airplane, the speed of the trim system and preference, and if trim is used, both the trim and the power come out as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

callout.text: Application: teach trim in a steep turn as two jobs, "trim in" once the bank and power are set and "trim out" as they come off. A student who trims in and forgets to trim out starts the next heading climbing.

check.q: In a left steep turn the ball sits to the right and the rate of turn is steady. Name it and give a fix.
check.a: The ball is toward the outside of the turn, so it is a skid [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]: too much rate for the bank. Relax the left rudder or increase the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

chunks.title: Risk: setting up and demonstrating errors safely

body.p: The PTS bars the evaluator from simulating any condition that may jeopardize safe flight or damage the airplane (CFII PTS, Introduction). Hold yourself to the same rule when you show a student an error. FII.VI.A covers the general hood-work rules; steep turns add these hazards:

bullets: Load and stall margin. Fly at or below VA or VO. Stall speed rises with load factor, and the margin between stall speed and maneuvering speed shrinks as the bank increases [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. A higher load factor makes stalls possible at seemingly safe airspeeds [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]], and sudden loss of control in a steep turn has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

The spiral. Overbanking without enough pitch ends in a diving spiral, where back pressure tightens the turn without raising the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Recover by shallowing the bank first; trying to recover from a steep nose-low bank with elevator alone steepens the bank and stresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

The inner ear. In a prolonged constant-rate turn the pilot feels no turn, the roll-out feels like a turn the other way, and a disoriented pilot may roll back in, sense a descent, pull and tighten the spiral [[23:72|IFH 3-5]] [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A head movement in a prolonged turn can set off the Coriolis illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

Traffic. Simulated instrument flight needs a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and see and avoid applies under IFR or VFR when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Clear before you start [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

60° of bank. When carrying anyone other than a crewmember, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank unless every occupant wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]; paragraph (d) lists exceptions such as flight tests for a certificate or rating [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]].

body.p: Before each error demo, brief it on the ground: the limits and the positive exchange of flight controls. Guard the controls, and when you must take over, say "I have the flight controls" calmly; anxious learners can be very strong [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Safety permitting, let the student go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but never past your own ability to perceive the problem, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Application: set numbers before the flight, for example an overbank demonstration no steeper than about 55°, a recovery started by 200 feet of altitude loss or a fast-rising airspeed, and a practice altitude that leaves room for a spiral or an accelerated stall. No source gives these numbers; they are instructor choices. Take control the moment a limit is reached.

check.q: Your student overbanks to 55°, the altimeter unwinds and she pulls harder. Why is pulling wrong, and what is the order of the recovery?
check.a: Past 45°, more back pressure mostly tightens the turn [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. Shallow the bank first with coordinated aileron and rudder, hold or relax the elevator, reduce power if the airspeed rises fast, then raise the nose once the elevator is effective [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

chunks.title: Common errors: pitch, bank and power

body.p: **Failure to recognize and make proper corrections for pitch, bank, or power errors.** The IFH says the steep turn errors are the same as the turn errors listed on IFH 7-25 and 7-26, and that they are more exaggerated, harder to correct and harder to analyze unless the rates of entry and recovery match the pilot's proficiency [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. FII.VI.B has the whole list; here is how each one looks in a steep turn. The PTS wants you to describe, recognize, analyze and correct them (CFII PTS, Satisfactory Performance); for each, say what you see, name it, give the cause and the fix.

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Altitude lost on entry
Altimeter, VSI and airspeed needles move fast as the bank comes in
Pitch not raised as vertical lift drops [[23:184|IFH 7-23]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], often from preoccupation with bank [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Check pitch as soon as bank pressure starts; nose up 3° to 5° with the roll [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Pitch raised too early or too much
A climb on entry, then a dive as she overcorrects
Slow cross-check and a fast roll-in: mechanical, premature back pressure, often with overcontrolling [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Slow the roll-in to the speed of her scan [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Overbanking
Bank past 50° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], altitude sagging, back pressure growing [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]
Overbanking tendency not held with opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]; overcontrolling on entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Opposite aileron once the bank is set [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]; bank pointer in every pass
Diving spiral
Altimeter and VSI falling fast, airspeed rising, despite back pressure [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]
Overbank without enough pitch; back pressure now tightens the turn [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]
Shallow the bank, hold or relax elevator, reduce power if needed, then raise the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]
Altitude fixed with back pressure alone
More pull, little climb, bank creeping
Not using bank to vary vertical lift [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Change bank about 5° together with the pitch [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Altitude gained on roll-out
A climb as the wings come level
Pitch not lowered and power not reduced with the bank [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Forward pressure to cruise pitch, power to the entry setting [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Airspeed decaying in the turn
Airspeed bleeding off as the nose comes up
No power for the extra drag [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]; airspeed not cross-checked as pitch changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Power as the bank passes 30° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; learn the power for the bank [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]
Erratic power
Throttle chasing the airspeed
Throttle friction, inaccurate settings, chasing the airspeed, abrupt pitch and bank changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
A known power setting for the bank, then small changes [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]

body.p: When pitch control is consistently late, stop the exercise: roll out, analyze, and go back to shallower turns before increasing the bank again [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Ask why it happened: some errors are slips that only need practice, others point to a method or habit to change [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: On every steep turn your student loses about 150 feet during the entry and then holds altitude well. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Failure to change pitch as the vertical lift drops, giving a consistent loss on entries [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Check pitch as soon as the bank pressure starts and raise the nose with the roll [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

chunks.title: Common error: precession of the horizon bar

body.p: **Failure to compensate for precession of the horizon bar of the attitude indicator.** Precession is the tilting or turning of a gyro in response to a deflective force [[1:217|PHAK 8-15]]. The attitude gyro must stay upright while the airplane rolls and pitches around it, but even low-friction bearings restrain it, causing precession that tilts it; an erection mechanism pushes it back toward vertical [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

bullets: What it does: a slight nose-up indication in a rapid acceleration, nose-down in a rapid deceleration, and a small bank and pitch error after a 180° turn. These errors are small and correct themselves within a minute or so after returning to straight-and-level [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
They are common and predictable, and the attitude indicator still shows pitch and bank in one glance with less visual effort and time than other flight instruments [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].
Because of precession, holding straight flight takes a precise check of the heading [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

body.p: What the student sees: after rolling out of a steep turn the attitude indicator shows wings level, but the heading indicator keeps turning. The IFH test: if the ball is centered, the attitude gyro has precessed; if it is not, the airplane may be slipping or skidding. Center the ball with rudder, check the attitude and heading indicators, stop the heading change if it continues, and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Missing it is an omission error: leveling with the attitude indicator alone and not checking the heading indicator [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

On glass: the AHRS display has no precession error [[23:199|IFH 7-38]], but the analog standby attitude indicator can tumble at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Older attitude indicators tumbled past about 60° of pitch or 100° of roll [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]; limits depend on the make and model [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

callout.text: Application: make the post-roll-out call "Wings level, heading steady, ball centered." If the heading is not steady with the wings level and the ball centered, the student stops the turn on the heading indicator and turn coordinator and treats the horizon bar as approximate until it settles, which the IFH says takes a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. To show it, fly a 180° steep turn yourself in VMC, the IFH's own example of this error [[23:146|IFH 6-13]], roll out on the attitude indicator alone, and have the student watch the heading indicator and ball.

check.q: After a 180° steep turn the attitude indicator shows level wings, the heading creeps left and the ball is centered. What is it, and what do you teach?
check.a: The attitude gyro has precessed. Stop the heading change, check the attitude and heading indicators and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; the error is small and corrects itself within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Common errors: uncoordinated controls and improper trim technique

body.p: **Uncoordinated use of controls.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Slip
Ball toward the inside of the turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Outer-wing drag [[24:75|AFH 3-14]], or a bank too steep for the rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Rudder on the side of the ball, or less bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Skid
Ball toward the outside of the turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Rate of turn too great for the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Relax rudder toward the turn, or more bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Adverse yaw at entry and roll-out
Nose swings away from the roll
Aileron without rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]
Rudder with every aileron input [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]
Throttle not coordinated with pitch and bank
Airspeed changes with each pitch and bank change
Slow cross-check, or turn aerodynamics not understood [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Power in step with the pitch: past 30° on entry, back to entry power on the roll-out [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Ball not checked
Turn coordinator looks right, ball out
Reading the miniature airplane alone [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Ball in every pass, especially if pressures are held [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]

body.p: **Improper trim technique.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Trim not used on entry
Heavy back pressure, tense hands, pitch wandering
Entry too fast for the cross-check [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; failure to trim during the entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Trim off the aft forces once power is set [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Trim and power left in
A climb and rising airspeed after the roll-out
Turn trim and power not removed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Trim in the roll-out callout; retrim as soon as practical [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Trim used to fly the turn
Pitch changed with the trim wheel
Trim and attitude/power changes confused [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Pressure first, then trim; trim alone gives erratic control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch follows the needle, hands tense
Overcontrolling hides the pressures to trim off [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Make the pitch change on the attitude indicator [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
No trim after power changes
Pitch drifts after the power is added
Failure to trim following power changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Application: say "power, then trim" as one step

body.p: Application, how to demonstrate them: in VMC first, briefly and at a safe altitude, hold a little extra rudder into a steep turn so the student sees the ball move to the outside and feels pushed toward the outside, then show a slip the other way [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. Keep it brief: held uncoordinated control deflections create the potential for a spin [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. For trim, fly one turn trimmed and one holding the force, as the IFH says an instructor can [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

callout.text: Application: an IFH-trained student holds a steep turn trimmed and nearly hands-off [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. If the student cannot let go for a second without the nose moving, the trim is wrong, not the student's strength.

check.q: Your student's right steep turn goes well, but after the roll-out the airplane climbs and speeds up. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Improper trim technique: the turn's trim and power were left in. Remove both as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], then retrim as soon as practical [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

chunks.title: Teaching it: building blocks and the talk-through

body.p: Plan it like any performance maneuver: only after the fundamentals are consistently good, with a detailed ground lesson first and building blocks that allow enough repetition [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. Known-to-unknown fits, since the steep turn is a turn the student already flies, with more bank [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Ground
Lift, load factor and overbanking, the steps, the errors, the limits and the exchange of controls [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Instructor tells, instructor does
Fly one each way while explaining power and attitudes in the order you briefed; if the demo strays, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Student tells, instructor does
She calls the steps and the scan, so you can check her understanding before the workload rises [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Student does, thinking aloud
Shallower turns first, then 45° [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]; correct errors in a positive and timely way [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Vary it
Reverse into the other direction, IFH step 8 [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], or combine it with other tasks to check understanding [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Partial panel
Application: only after full panel is solid, with modest banks
Debrief
Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

body.p: **A talk-through for S1**, primary-and-supporting words, round dials, left 360° from 270°:

bullets: "Clearing turns done [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. Entry speed at or below maneuvering speed for today's weight [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]."
"Coordinated left aileron and rudder, rolling in only as fast as I can scan [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]."
"Vertical lift is going away, so back pressure as the bank comes in: nose up about 3 to 5 degrees [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]."
"Passing 30, power up to hold the airspeed [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]."
"Forty-five on the bank scale. Opposite aileron to stop the overbanking, rudder to keep the ball centered [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]."
"Trim off the back pressure [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. Attitude indicator holds the bank, altimeter for pitch, airspeed for power [[23:199|IFH 7-38]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."
"Thirty feet low: a few degrees less bank and a touch more back pressure, together [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]."
"Passing 290, roll out at the same rate: nose to cruise pitch, power back, trim out [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]."
"Wings level on 270. Heading steady? Ball centered? If the heading creeps with the wings level and the ball centered, the gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]."

body.p: In control-and-performance words: set 45° and the higher pitch on the attitude indicator and the extra power on the power gauge, trim, cross-check the altimeter, VSI and airspeed, adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]. Partial panel: "Turn coordinator past the standard-rate mark, ball centered; altimeter, VSI and airspeed for pitch, small inputs only; compass once I am level [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]." On glass: "Roll pointer on the 45° index, altitude trend and VSI tape for pitch, airspeed tape for power [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]."

callout.text: The PTS lists an explanation that needs prompting as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (CFII PTS, Unsatisfactory Performance). Application: rehearse this script under the hood until the numbers come without thinking.

check.q: In the "student tells, instructor does" step, why does the AIH have the student talk you through the steep turn?
check.a: Free of flying, she organizes the steps and techniques, and you can check her understanding and correct a misunderstanding before she is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Analyze and correct: when the examiner flies the errors

body.p: For S2 the evaluator plays the student and flies errors on purpose. The PTS counts competence in describing, recognizing, analyzing and correcting them toward a pass (CFII PTS, Satisfactory Performance). Use the same four steps every time: what you see, the error's name, its cause, the fix.

head: Simulated error
What you say
rows: Rolls to 45°, nose stays put, altimeter unwinds
"Altitude loss on entry: no pitch change as the vertical lift dropped. Nose up 3 to 5 degrees as you roll in" [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]
Lets the bank creep to 55° and pulls
"Overbank: past 45°, pulling only tightens the turn. Less bank first, then pitch" [[23:215|IFH 7-54]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Rolls out on the attitude indicator; heading keeps changing, ball centered
"Precessed gyro: stop the turn on the heading indicator, check the ball, retrim" [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Holds the turn with rudder pushed into it
"Skid, ball outside: relax the rudder or add bank" [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Leaves trim and power in after the roll-out
"Turn trim and power still in: take both out" [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Never adds power
"Airspeed bleeding: power as you pass 30 degrees" [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. Some errors are slips that only need practice; others show a method or habit to change [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. If the student flies it well but you doubt she understands why, have her vary the maneuver or combine it with another; a student who does not understand the principles will probably not manage it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Any action or lack of action that makes the evaluator step in to keep the flight safe is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (CFII PTS, Unsatisfactory Performance). If a simulated error develops toward a real hazard, say so and take control by the briefed procedure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: The evaluator, as your student, rolls out of a steep turn on the attitude indicator alone and the heading keeps changing with the ball centered. What four things do you say?
check.a: What you see (heading changing with the wings level and the ball centered), the name (failure to compensate for precession of the horizon bar), the cause (the gyro precessed and the heading was not checked [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]), and the fix: stop the heading change, check the instruments, retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

scenario.title: Steep turns in the club's vacuum-gyro trainer
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot with 15 hours of instrument training, flies the club's fixed-pitch four-seat trainer with a six-pack panel, one vacuum pump for the attitude and heading indicators and an electric turn coordinator. Today she is light, with two aboard and half fuel. The weather is good VMC with scattered cumulus well above the practice area, which lies under a busy approach path. The plan: steep turns under the view-limiting device, full panel first, then partial panel.

questions.q: On the ground, what bank and entry speed do you brief, and why not simply the maximum-weight VA from the POH?
questions.a: Use the IFH 45° steep turn [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], entered at or below VA or VO because of the higher load factors [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. VA is lower at light weight, for example 90 knots instead of 100 [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], so today the maximum-weight figure is too fast. Brief the limits and the positive exchange of flight controls too [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: On her first left turn, as the bank passes 30° the altimeter and VSI start down and the airspeed rises. What happened, and what do you say?
questions.a: The vertical lift dropped and she did not raise the pitch; pitch control is usually the hardest part of a steep turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Coach: "Nose up 3 to 5 degrees as you roll in, and speed up your scan" [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

questions.q: She pulls harder. The bank creeps to 55°, the altimeter unwinds faster and the airspeed keeps rising. What is it and what happens now?
questions.a: A diving spiral from overbanking: back pressure is now tightening the turn [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Take control if the briefed limit is reached [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, hold or relax the elevator, reduce power if the airspeed rises fast, then raise the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]; elevator alone would steepen the bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: Later, after a good 180° steep turn, she rolls out on the attitude indicator. It shows level wings, but the heading indicator keeps creeping and the ball is centered. What is it, and what do you teach?
questions.a: Precession of the horizon bar: with the ball centered and the heading changing, the attitude gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. It is an omission error, leveling on the attitude indicator alone [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Stop the turn on the heading indicator and turn coordinator and retrim; the error corrects itself within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

questions.q: You cover the attitude and heading indicators. How does her steep turn change?
questions.a: Steep now means past standard rate [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], so she holds the turn coordinator past the standard-rate mark; it shows rate, not bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. Pitch comes from the rate of the altimeter needle, the VSI and airspeed, with small inputs only [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]], and the heading from the clock and compass once level [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Keep the bank modest.

questions.q: In the debrief she says the whole flight was bad. How do you run it?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], grading each element rather than just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Then sort the errors with her: some are slips that only need practice, others point to a method or habit to change, for example a late entry pitch that comes from not understanding the lift loss [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly a steep turn each way by instruments while explaining the entry, the pitch and power changes, the overbanking tendency, trim, the roll-out lead and the post-roll-out precession check, full panel and partial panel.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], explaining in the same order you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Start with shallower banks and build to 45° [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

skills.do: When the evaluator loses altitude on entry, overbanks, rolls out on a precessed gyro, skids, or leaves the trim and power in, say what you see, name the error, explain the cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH 7-25 and 7-26 faults in a steep turn at a safe altitude, inside limits you brief beforehand [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

quiz.q: Your student asks what makes a turn "steep" in instrument training. What does the IFH say?
options: Any turn at 30° of bank or more
Any turn greater than standard rate
Only a turn steeper than 50° of bank
A turn flown at the 25° holding bank
quiz.why: For instrument training in conventional airplanes, any turn greater than standard rate is steep, and the exact bank where a turn becomes steep is unimportant [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. 50° is where the IFH says overbanking starts [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], not where a steep turn starts.

quiz.q: Your student asks how much heavier she will feel in a level 45° steep turn. What does the AFH say?
options: About 1.41 times her weight, in any airplane
About 2 times, but less in a faster airplane
About 1.15 times, the same as at standard rate
It depends on airspeed, not bank
quiz.why: For a given bank in a level turn the same load factor is always produced, whatever the airspeed or airplane: 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Airspeed changes the rate and radius of turn, not the load factor [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: Your student holds a little aileron into a 45° turn, as she does at 20°, and the bank keeps steepening. Why?
options: Adverse yaw from the down aileron keeps rolling the airplane in
P-factor rolls the airplane into the turn at a high angle of attack
At about 45° the airplane keeps rolling unless she holds opposite aileron
The attitude gyro has precessed and shows less bank than she really has
quiz.why: At about 45° or more the airplane continues in the direction of the bank even with neutral controls unless opposite aileron is held [[24:73|AFH 3-12]], because the outer wing flies faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Adverse yaw yaws the nose away from the turn, not into it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: In the IFH glass steep turn procedure, when is power added?
options: Before the roll-in is started
Once the turn is trimmed hands-off
When the airspeed is 5 knots slow
As the bank rolls past 30°
quiz.why: Step 3: as the bank rolls past 30°, increase power to maintain the entry airspeed [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The AFH also adds power as the bank is established, generally before 30° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Waiting for the airspeed to drop is reacting late.

quiz.q: In Figure 7-36 the turn coordinator's miniature airplane sits past the standard-rate mark with the ball centered. What does that tell your student?
options: The turn is faster than standard rate and coordinated; it does not give the bank
The airplane is banked exactly 45°, so the attitude indicator need not be checked
The airplane is skidding, so she should relax some of the rudder into the turn
The turn coordinator has failed and should be covered for the rest of the flight
quiz.why: The turn coordinator shows only rate and direction of turn, not a specific bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]; a centered ball means coordinated flight [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. Past standard rate is exactly what the IFH calls a steep turn [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

quiz.q: On a PFD your student is 100 feet low in a 45° turn, pulls harder, and the nose barely rises. What does the IFH tell her to do?
options: Hold the bank and pull harder until the trend turns
Reduce the bank about 5° while adjusting back pressure
Lower the nose to gain speed, then pull back up to altitude
Add full power and hold both the bank and the pitch
quiz.why: When correcting altitude it is imperative to modify the bank about ±5° to vary the vertical component of lift, not just adjust back pressure, and to do both at once. Past 45°, more back pressure only tightens the turn radius [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

quiz.q: Where does the IFH glass procedure start the roll-out from a 45° steep turn?
options: About 5° before the heading
Exactly on the heading
About 20° before the heading
About 45° before the new heading
quiz.why: Step 5: begin rolling out approximately 20° prior to the desired heading [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The AFH rule of half the bank gives 22.5° at 45° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], so both are close.

quiz.q: After a 180° steep turn the attitude indicator shows level wings, the heading creeps, and the ball is centered. What is happening?
options: The airplane is slipping
The turn coordinator has failed
The heading indicator has drifted
The attitude gyro has precessed
quiz.why: If the heading indicator shows a change in heading while the attitude indicator shows level flight and the ball is centered, the attitude gyro has precessed; with the ball off center it may be a slip or skid [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

quiz.q: What does the IFH say about the size and duration of the attitude indicator's error after a 180° turn?
options: Small; it corrects within a minute or so of level flight
Large; the gyro must be caged and erected again
Small, but it stays until the next engine start
Large enough that the gyro must be covered
quiz.why: There may be a small bank angle and pitch error after a 180° turn; these inherent errors are small and correct themselves within a minute or so after returning to straight-and-level flight [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: Your student slips in a right steep turn. Where is the ball, and what is one fix?
options: Left, outside the turn; relax right rudder or add bank
Right, inside the turn; relax right rudder or add bank
Left, outside the turn; add more right rudder or reduce bank
Right, inside the turn; add right rudder or reduce bank
quiz.why: A slip shows the ball toward the inside of the turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. Add rudder on the side toward the turn or reduce the bank; relaxing rudder or adding bank is the fix for a skid [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH say to fly steep turns at or below VA or VO?
options: So the airplane stalls before it exceeds the design load limit
So the turn radius stays small enough to see the entry point
So the overbanking tendency goes away at the lower airspeed
So the airspeed stays inside the green arc all through the steep turn
quiz.why: Because of higher load factors, steep turns are flown at or below VA or VO; at those speeds the airplane stalls before exceeding the design load limit [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The overbanking tendency depends on bank and airspeed but does not go away [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: The AFH says the certification standards do not require trim in a steep turn. If your student trims, what must she remember?
options: Trim only after the roll-out, never in the turn
Use rudder trim only; elevator trim is unsafe here
Leave the trim set for the next steep turn
Take out the trim and the power at the end
quiz.why: If trim is used, pilots should not forget to remove both the trim and the power inputs as the maneuver is completed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The IFH steps trim off the aft forces in the turn and retrim as soon as practical after it [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

final_quiz.q: Per the IFH, practicing steep turns by instruments prepares a pilot for what?
options: Holding patterns flown at the AIM bank limit
Quick, confident reactions to unexpected attitudes
Circling approaches at minimums in low visibility
Spin recovery by reference to instruments alone
final_quiz.why: Practicing steep turns increases proficiency in the basic skills and enables smooth, quick and confident reactions to unexpected abnormal flight attitudes under instrument conditions [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: On round dials, as your student rolls into a steep turn, the altimeter, VSI and airspeed needles all move fast. What does the IFH say causes this?
options: Precession of the attitude gyro during the fast roll-in
A static port blanked off by the very steep bank angle
Loss of vertical lift not met by a pitch increase
Adverse yaw from aileron held into the turn
final_quiz.why: Unless immediately corrected with a pitch increase, the loss of vertical lift results in rapid movement of the altimeter, vertical speed and airspeed needles; the faster the bank changes, the more suddenly the lift changes [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

final_quiz.q: Figure 7-37: altimeter and VSI falling fast, airspeed rising, the student holding back pressure. What is the first recovery action?
options: Pull harder to raise the nose first, then shallow the bank
Roll quickly into the opposite bank
Reduce power to idle and pull to the stall warning
Shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder
final_quiz.why: In a diving spiral, immediately shallow the bank with smooth, coordinated aileron and rudder, hold or slightly relax elevator pressure, reduce power if the airspeed increase is rapid, then raise the nose when the elevator is effective [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Elevator alone steepens the bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's pitch control is late on every steep turn entry. What does the IFH recommend?
options: Roll out, analyze, then practice shallower turns first
Keep flying 45° turns until the timing comes by itself
Use a faster roll-in so the turn is set before altitude goes
Add nose-up trim before the roll-in to preload the pitch
final_quiz.why: If pitch control is consistently late on entries, roll out immediately and analyze; practice shallower turns first, then increase the bank as cross-check and control improve [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. A faster roll makes the lift change more sudden [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the IFH want the pitch attitude kept relatively constant once the steep turn is established?
options: It lets the attitude gyro erect during the turn
It frees time for cross-check and interpretation
It holds the load factor under 1.41 at any bank
It stops the overbanking tendency without aileron
final_quiz.why: During steep turn training, attend to the most important tasks first; keep the pitch attitude relatively constant, and more time can be devoted to cross-check and instrument interpretation [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: During the recovery from a steep turn, what does the IFH say must happen to elevator and power?
options: Hold back pressure and power until the wings are level
Add power as the bank comes off to keep the airspeed up
Release back pressure and reduce power in step with bank
Release the back pressure only once the new heading is captured
final_quiz.why: During recovery, elevator and power control must be coordinated with bank control in proportion to the changes in aerodynamic forces: back elevator pressure released and power decreased [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Holding them causes the consistent altitude gain on roll-outs [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: On a PFD your student's bank creeps from 45° to 53° as she pulls to stop a descent. What is this, and why is pulling a problem?
options: Normal drift; the PFD will hold the bank at 60° by itself
Precession; the AHRS bank display lags at high bank angles
A skid; too much rudder into the turn for the bank she has
Overbanking; past 45° pulling tightens the turn more than it lifts
final_quiz.why: The IFH calls a bank past 50° overbanking; past 45° the horizontal lift is the greater force, and more back pressure only tightens the turn radius [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. The PFD only extends the roll index past 60° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], and the AHRS has no precession error [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's airplane stalls at 50 knots in level flight. About what is its stall speed in a level 60° turn, per the AFH?
options: About 70 knots
About 60 knots
About 100 knots
About 50 knots
final_quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: an airplane that stalls at 50 knots level stalls at 60 knots at 45° and at 70 knots at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your student flies steep turns on a PFD and asks whether she still needs to check for horizon bar precession. What is accurate?
options: Yes; the AHRS precesses more than a vacuum gyro does
Not on the AHRS display, but yes with the standby gyro
No; neither the PFD nor the standby gyro can ever precess
Only past 60° of bank, where the PFD declutters
final_quiz.why: EFDs eliminate the precession error of analog gyros [[23:199|IFH 7-38]], but the analog standby attitude indicator is still a gyro and can tumble at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]; analog attitude indicators show a small error after a 180° turn [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: Gyros covered, your student wants to fly a partial panel steep turn. What makes it "steep" for this training?
options: A ball held one width to the inside of the turn
A compass card turning faster than 10° per second
A turn coordinator past the standard-rate mark
A 45° bank read from the turn coordinator marks
final_quiz.why: Any turn greater than standard rate is steep for instrument training [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The turn coordinator shows only rate and direction of turn, not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], so it cannot show 45°.

final_quiz.q: In the IFH example glass airplane, the AHRS fails during a steep turn. Which statement is accurate?
options: The PFD keeps attitude but loses the heading display
The autopilot keeps every mode, so it can fly the turn
The standby gyro cannot tumble at any bank angle
The slip/skid indicator is lost, with no standby turn coordinator
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications and all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold; the slip/skid indicator is gone and there is no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The analog standby attitude indicator can tumble at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

final_quiz.q: In a right steep turn your student says she feels pushed toward the inside of the turn. What is happening?
options: A slip, with the ball toward the inside of the turn
A skid, with the ball toward the outside of the turn
Nothing; it is the extra load factor of the steep bank
A skid, with the ball toward the inside of the turn
final_quiz.why: A pilot feels pressed toward the outside of a turn in a skid and toward the inside in a slip [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]; in a slip the ball is toward the inside of the turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your student starts to lose altitude in a steep turn during practice. Which AIH guidance fits?
options: Take the controls at the first sign of any error
Safety permitting, let her work part of the way out
Say nothing until the debrief so she can keep flying
Let her continue until she exceeds the airplane limits
final_quiz.why: Correction of learner errors does not mean taking over immediately; safety permitting, it is frequently better to let learners progress part of the way into the mistake and find a way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Learners should never exceed the instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which distraction would you avoid in the middle of a prolonged steep turn under the hood, and why?
options: Reading the OAT; it is too easy to be a real test
Resetting the clock; it stops at high load factors
Picking up a pencil; head movement can cause Coriolis
A 200-foot climb; it is a VFR-only distraction
final_quiz.why: In a prolonged turn, a head movement in a different plane can trigger the Coriolis illusion; retrieve dropped items with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Dropping a pencil is one of the AIH distraction examples [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]; use it in straight flight.

final_quiz.q: Your student's right steep turn is trimmed well and rolls out on heading, then the airplane climbs 150 feet and speeds up. What was missed?
options: Adding right rudder for the outer wing's drag
Leading the roll-out by half the bank angle
Checking the attitude gyro for precession
Taking out the turn's trim and power
final_quiz.why: If trim is used, remove both the trim and the power inputs as the maneuver is completed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; the IFH steps reduce power to the entry setting and retrim [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. A missed lead would show as a heading error, not a climb.

final_quiz.q: On your CFII checkride the evaluator, as your student, rolls out of a steep turn on the attitude indicator alone and the heading keeps changing. What does the PTS expect of you?
options: Recognize and name the error, explain the cause, give the fix
Say nothing, since only your own flying is graded in flight
Take the controls and fly the rest of the Task yourself
Wait for the debrief, since errors are graded on the ground
final_quiz.why: The PTS counts competence in describing, recognizing, analyzing and correcting common errors simulated by the evaluator (CFII PTS, Satisfactory Performance). Here: omission of the heading indicator after a steep turn hides precession [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]; stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

takeaways: Any turn past standard rate is steep for instrument training; the IFH example uses 45°.
Past 45° the airplane keeps rolling, and back pressure alone tightens the turn; use bank and pitch together to fix altitude.
Roll in: nose up 3 to 5 degrees, power past 30°, opposite aileron, trim. Roll out about 20° early: nose down, power back, trim out.
Pitch is the hard part. Speed the scan up on entry and roll-out, and teach shallower turns first.
Diving spiral: shallow the bank first, then raise the nose.
After every roll-out check heading and ball; level wings with a turning heading and a centered ball means a precessed gyro.
Partial panel: the turn coordinator shows rate, not bank. Keep banks modest and inputs small.
Demonstrate errors only inside limits you brief: at or below VA for the weight, and a bank limit you choose, well short of 60°.
cfi_notes: Roll-out lead: the IFH glass procedure says about 20° before the heading [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], the AFH says half the bank [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], 22.5° at 45°, and the IFH turn rule is also half the bank, refined by practice [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. They agree within a few degrees; teach one and let the student calibrate it.

The IFH glass section says analog instruments have no 45° index, so the bank must be approximated [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], yet its own analog attitude indicator figure marks 10°, 20°, 30°, 45° and 60° [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], and IFH 7-7 says some dials are graduated only every 30° [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Check the dial in your airplane before you brief the bank.

Altitude corrections differ in emphasis. The IFH says it is imperative to vary the bank ±5° along with back pressure [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; the AFH fixes minor pitch errors with elevator while holding the bank, and for a large nose-low loss reduces the bank first [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Both reject pulling alone in a steep, nose-low bank.

Pitch and power timing: the IFH glass steps raise the pitch 3° to 5° immediately and add power as the bank passes 30° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; the AFH adds back pressure and power generally before 30° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Trim: the IFH says use it, and an instructor can demonstrate with and without it [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; the AFH says the certification standards do not require it, and if used both trim and power must come out at the end [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

The AFH lists "performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references" as a steep turn error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. That is for the VFR maneuver of AI.IX.A; in this Task the instruments are the reference. Do not let the two lists confuse a dual-rated student.

No source labels the primary instruments for a steep turn. The IFH makes the attitude indicator primary when a specific bank is flown [[23:199|IFH 7-38]], the altimeter primary for pitch in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] and the airspeed indicator primary for power at constant airspeed in a turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Be ready to explain your choice if you use primary and supporting.

The IFH glass section still refers to the instrument PTS when it says steep turns are not required on the checkride [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. The CFII PTS lists FAA-S-ACS-8 among the Task references; teach from the current handbook and do not quote checkride content from memory.

Glass removes precession from the PFD [[23:199|IFH 7-38]], but partial panel on glass means the analog standby attitude indicator, which can tumble at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Teach the precession check on every airplane that has an analog gyro.
gaps: No source gives the pitch attitude, power setting or entry speed for a steep turn in a particular airplane; take them from the POH/AFM and VA or VO for the actual weight.
No source describes a partial panel steep turn in detail, or how far the turn coordinator deflects at a given bank; calibrate it full panel in your airplane.
The CFII PTS gives no tolerances for this Task, and no source here gives altitude, bank or airspeed limits for an instrument steep turn.
No source gives a minimum altitude for practicing instrument steep turns or for demonstrating overbanking and the spiral.
The IFH says the attitude indicator error after a 180° turn corrects within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]; no source gives the size of the error after a 360° or 720° steep turn.
No source here gives the bank limits of the standby attitude indicator in a particular glass airplane; check the AFM supplement.

activities.title: Numbers behind the steep turn
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A trainer stalls at 50 knots in level flight. Per the AFH, about what is its stall speed in a level 45° steep turn?
items.why: The AFH example gives 60 knots at 45°. The method: stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and 50 x the square root of 1.41 is about 59 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

items.q: Using the PHAK formula, rate of turn = 1,091 x tan(bank) / TAS in knots, what is the rate of turn at 45° of bank and 120 knots TAS? (tan 45° = 1)
items.why: 1,091 x 1 / 120 = 9.1° per second [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]: three times standard rate, which is why the roll-out comes up so fast.

items.q: At that rate, about how many seconds does a 360° steep turn take?
items.why: 360 / 9.1 = about 40 seconds, the PHAK method of dividing 360° by the rate of turn [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

items.q: A left 360° steep turn starts on 090°. Using the IFH glass lead, at what heading do you start the roll-out?
items.why: Begin rolling out about 20° before the desired heading [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]. Turning left, the heading counts down to 090°, so start at 110°.

items.q: A right 360° steep turn at 50° of bank starts on 180°. Using the AFH rule of half the bank, at what heading do you start the roll-out?
items.why: Lead by half the bank, 25°; turning right, the heading counts up to 180°, so start at 155° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

activities.title: True or false: lift, load and overbanking
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: At about 30° of bank most airplanes keep rolling into the turn unless opposite aileron is held.
cards.why: False. Between about 20° and 45° the airplane tends to hold the bank with neutral aileron; the overbanking tendency starts at about 45° or more [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

cards.s: In a level turn, the load factor for a given bank is the same in every airplane at every airspeed.
cards.why: True. For a given bank in a level turn the same load factor is always produced: 1.41 at 45°, 2.0 at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

cards.s: The faster outer wing's extra drag causes a slight slip in a steep turn, corrected with rudder.
Past 45° of bank, more back pressure alone is the best way to stop an altitude loss.
cards.why: False. Past 45° the horizontal lift is the greater force, and more back pressure only tightens the turn; change the bank about 5° along with the pitch [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

cards.s: A level turn at 75° of bank exceeds the 3.8 load factor a standard category GA airplane is designed for.

activities.title: The IFH steep turn, step by step
activities.intro: Put the IFH glass steep turn steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Roll into a coordinated 45° bank and raise the pitch about 3° to 5°
As the bank passes 30°, add power to hold the entry airspeed
Trim off the aft control wheel forces
Start the roll-out about 20° before the desired heading
Apply forward pressure to the level cruise pitch attitude
Reduce power to the entry setting
Retrim, or continue into a steep turn the other way
activities.why: Steps 1 to 8 of the IFH steep turn on an electronic flight display [[23:215|IFH 7-54]].

activities.title: Which panel is it?
activities.intro: Tap each item, then the setup it belongs to.

items.t: Bank may have to be estimated on a dial marked only every 30°
Check the horizon bar for precession after the roll-out
Roll precisely to the 45° index on the roll scale
Altitude trend indicator shows the loss as the bank comes in
Roll index extends past 60° to show the way back to level
Hold the turn coordinator past the standard-rate mark
Pitch from the altimeter needle's rate, the VSI and airspeed only
No slip/skid indicator in the IFH example airplane

activities.why: Analog dials and precession [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; glass 45° index, trend indicators and the extended roll index [[23:215|IFH 7-54]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]; partial panel [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]] [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

activities.title: Slip, skid or a precessed gyro?
activities.intro: Tap each clue, then what it points to.

items.t: Ball toward the inside of the turn
Banked too much for the rate of turn
Feels pressed toward the inside of the turn
Ball toward the outside of the turn
Rate of turn too great for the bank
Feels pressed toward the outside of the turn
Wings level on the attitude indicator, heading turning, ball centered
Small bank error after a 180° turn that fades within a minute or so

activities.why: Ball position [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]; slip and skid causes [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]; the feel [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]; precession [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

activities.title: Name the fix
activities.intro: Tap what you see from the right seat, then the fix you coach.

pairs.r: Nose up 3° to 5° as the bank comes in
Forward pressure and power back with the bank

pairs.l: Altimeter and VSI falling fast, airspeed rising
pairs.r: Shallow the bank first, then raise the nose
Hold opposite aileron once the bank is set

pairs.l: Climb and speed gain after the roll-out
pairs.r: Take out the turn's trim and power

pairs.l: Airspeed bleeding off in the turn
pairs.r: Add power as the bank passes 30°

activities.why: Entry and roll-out pitch [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; diving spiral [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]; overbanking [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; trim and power [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

activities.title: Read the attitude indicator
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the attitude indicator.

pins.label: Bank pointer, read against the scale
The IFH steep turn bank; only a dot here
Bank where a level turn pulls 2 G
Can show a small error after a 180° turn
Wings and dot span about 2° of pitch
Raises or lowers the miniature airplane

activities.why: Bank scale and pointer, the 2° miniature airplane and the adjustment knob [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]; 45° steep turn [[23:215|IFH 7-54]]; 2 G at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; error after a 180° turn [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

activities.title: A steep turn lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFII with an instrument student in a light, vacuum-gyro trainer. The weather is good VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: Before the flight she plans to use the maximum-weight VA from the POH as her entry speed.
options: Use it; VA is one fixed number for the airplane
Use VA for today's light weight, which is lower
Use 10 knots above VA for extra stall margin
Use any airspeed in the green arc for the entry
steps.why: Steep turns are flown at or below VA or VO [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], and VA is lower when the airplane is light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

steps.s: Hood on, first left steep turn. She sets 45° exactly, but the altimeter and VSI start down.
options: Have her hold the bank and just watch the altimeter
Take control at once and end the steep turn lesson
Coach: nose up 3 to 5 degrees, and scan faster
Have her add rudder into the turn to raise the nose
steps.why: Pitch must come up as the vertical lift drops, usually 3° to 5° [[23:215|IFH 7-54]], and the cross-check must speed up as the turn steepens [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

steps.s: Next turn: bank 55°, altimeter unwinding, airspeed rising. She pulls harder and the nose will not come up.
options: Shallow the bank first, then raise the nose
Pull harder until the altimeter needle stops
Add full power to climb out of the descent
Roll quickly into the opposite steep bank
steps.why: A diving spiral: shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, hold or relax the elevator, reduce power if needed, then raise the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Elevator alone steepens the bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

steps.s: After a good 360° the attitude indicator shows level wings, but the heading keeps creeping and the ball is centered.
options: Call it a vacuum failure and cover the attitude gyro
Precession: stop the turn on the heading indicator and retrim
A slip: add rudder toward the ball and reduce the bank
Ignore it; heading indicators drift 15° per hour anyway
steps.why: With the ball centered and the heading changing while the attitude indicator shows level, the attitude gyro has precessed: stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

steps.s: Next lesson she asks how steep to make her partial panel steep turns.
options: 45°, read from the turn coordinator's marks
60°, so the exercise is truly realistic
Modestly past the standard-rate mark
Standard rate only; steep needs a gyro
steps.why: Any turn past standard rate is steep for instrument training [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and the turn coordinator shows rate, not bank [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. Application: keep it modest.
